topic: we need to brainstorm solutions to generating regen or Newgen faces but of a higher realistic quality than fm does and the possibility of aging what is the solution space research solutions and think extensively before we start brainstorming

areas.name: What more realistic than Football Manager means, and where faces show
areas.brief: Decided: the first version solves the plastic look and the clones best; photoreal by default with a painted setting; the profile sets the bar. Open: whether the youth intake reveal needs more.

areas.name: Aging, and the same person across a whole life
areas.brief: Decided: aging runs 15 to 70, all in the 3D head; faces update at career stages with two academy stages; weight after football and stress greying mark the face; hair loss goes first if art forces a cut. Core and first version: all four. Top risk: none named.

areas.name: Faces that fit where a player comes from
areas.brief: Decided: real countries; all four origin failures unacceptable; a mix of ancestry over about 20 regional gene pools; spreads follow footballers, from population data shifted by public heritage records; heritage gives international eligibility. Core and first version: all four. Later: family looks. Top risk: none named.

areas.name: Player trust: the backlash against AI art, store disclosure, and likeness to real people
areas.brief: Decided: generative AI in scope with Steam disclosure; studio audits check likeness before release; no AI claim for the painted mode; open by design in the store, settings, and a public page. Core: disclosure, audits, openness. First version: all four. Top risk: none named.

areas.name: Scale, save size, and the player's hardware
areas.brief: Open: where the photo finish runs. A genome is a few hundred bytes per player; only the photo finish needs a graphics card.

areas.name: A shipped library of finished face images
areas.brief: Not the lead: a finished image cannot age. It returns only as a studio library of textures.

areas.name: Generative AI, on the player's PC or in the studio
areas.brief: Decided: our best render with studio textures is the default; an optional download adds an AI finish on capable PCs (Vega with a depth adapter, then our own distilled finisher); players without it choose painted or render; studio audits check likeness. Core and first version: all four. Top risk: the finisher is too slow on real PCs.

areas.name: A face genome rendered as a 3D head
areas.brief: Decided: FLAME 2023 Open shape with MakeHuman CC0 targets, age fully in 3D; hair cards, dedicated coiled styles, 150+ styles changed at life moments; code structure with studio AI textures shipped as data, one reviewer; a Rust portrait process, followed players baked at age bands, others on demand; a no-AI painted shader. Core and first version: all. Top risk: the art job.

areas.name: Procedural 2D faces
areas.brief: Not the lead. faces.js stays a reference for how small a face record can be.

areas.name: A genome render with an AI realism pass on top
areas.brief: Decided: the lead route. Identity and age live in the 3D head; an optional AI finish paints skin and light. Core and first version.

areas.name: Bought character middleware
areas.brief: Not the lead: FaceGen was set aside for FLAME plus MakeHuman; MetaHuman cannot create heads during play.

areas.name: Licences and the MIT or Apache rule
areas.brief: Verified clear: FLAME 2023 Open, MakeHuman assets, faces.js. Open: FLAME skin textures and the tools that guide the AI pass.

threads.name: Regen faces more realistic than Football Manager, that age
The face genome with an AI finish

items.text: Player records today carry no nationality, birth date, or appearance fields, and the season design plans no youth intake yet, so a face system also defines the identity data it rests on.
items.evidence: crates/engine/src (no match for nationality, birth, or appearance); docs/design/realism/03-season-layer.md

items.text: The product rule says brand assets and illustration are generated in code, not sourced from image files, and every dependency must be MIT- or Apache-compatible.
Football Manager added 2D generated regen faces in 2008 and 3D faces in 2018; the 2026 edition moved to Unity, and players still call regen faces plastic and uncanny.
No source describes any aging of Football Manager regen faces; a regen keeps one face from debut to retirement.
The popular fan mods assign pre-made StyleGAN photos to regens from about 14 appearance folders by player ID; the faces never age, and the tools are GPL-3.0.
EA FC youth players come from a small bank of heads; players complain of clones and of faces that never grow a beard or age.
Out of the Park Baseball uses FaceGen 3D heads whose faces age and change with weight across a career: the one sports-management precedent for aging faces.

Crusader Kings 3 stores each character as a DNA string of gene sliders, children inherit genes from both parents, and age is a separate layer of blend shapes and wrinkle and hair-loss textures over the same head; a small team built it.
faces.js, the procedural SVG face generator of Basketball GM, stores a face as a small object and is Apache-2.0.
StyleGAN weights carry NVIDIA's non-commercial licence and the FFHQ face set is CC BY-NC-SA, so the classic photoreal face GAN is closed to a commercial game.
FLUX.1 schnell is Apache-2.0 and makes an image in about four steps; FLUX.1 dev is non-commercial; SDXL and SDXL-Lightning allow commercial use under an OpenRAIL licence; SDXL-Turbo does not.

Almost every tool that keeps one identity across images (InstantID, IP-Adapter FaceID, PhotoMaker, PuLID) depends on InsightFace face-recognition weights, which are non-commercial without a paid licence.
The strong learned aging models (SAM, Lifespan Age Transformation Synthesis, HRFAE, CUSP) are built on StyleGAN or on non-commercial face sets; newer diffusion aging work has unclear weight licences.
An age slider can be a small add-on to an image model (Concept Sliders), with a few megabytes per slider, on any base model the studio may use commercially.
The FLAME 2023 Open head model allows commercial use under CC-BY-4.0; the Basel Face Model and SMPL-X are non-commercial without a paid licence.
Since 2025, MetaHuman heads may be used in any engine for commercial work under the Unreal licence terms; Character Creator content forbids an in-game character creator without an enterprise licence.
MakeHuman code is AGPL, but its assets and its exports are CC0, so it can serve as an offline tool whose output ships.
Images that Blender renders are not covered by its GPL, so an offline render step is licence-safe while Blender itself stays out of the shipped game.
About half of Steam players have a graphics card with 8 GB or more; a mid-range card makes a four-step portrait in seconds, and integrated graphics or CPU-only machines take minutes.
Hosted four-step generation costs roughly 3 to 25 dollars per thousand images.
A library of 50,000 faces at four ages and about 80 KB each is about 16 GB, while a face genome is a few hundred bytes per player.
items.evidence: estimate from typical WebP portrait sizes

items.text: Steam asks every game to disclose player-facing AI content; content generated while the game runs also needs a written account of its guardrails.
Games accused of AI art on Steam in 2025 and 2026 met review bombs and lost awards and sponsors.
The EU AI Act labelling duty for images that resemble real people started on 2 August 2026; a wholly fictional face that resembles nobody should fall outside it.
Diffusion models can reproduce training photos of real people; a similarity check against known faces, and a hard exclusion of real footballers, is the standard defence.
Football Manager players repeatedly complain of faces that do not fit a regen's nation, and of skin tone buckets too coarse to tell regions apart.
The common face training set is about two thirds white, and models trained on it drift towards lighter faces.

Facial bone growth ends at about 18 to 21 in men; fine lines show in the 30s and sagging in the 40s; about half of men show hair loss by 50 and four in five by 70; greying starts in the mid-30s to mid-40s depending on ancestry.
The low-drift aging pipeline makes a few anchor ages from one identity and blends between them, instead of making each age again from scratch.

Store each player as a face genome, render it as a 3D head for identity and age, then run a light AI pass over the render for photoreal skin and hair; identity comes from the geometry, not from a face-recognition model.
Regens can inherit genes from a retired player, so a son or a nephew of a club legend looks like him.
Life events mark the face: a broken nose after a clash, weight after retirement, a beard phase, a touchline manager who greys over a long reign.
The player chooses a portrait style in settings: photoreal, or a drawn style with no AI in it.
Realism matters most on the player profile and the youth intake screen; squad lists show faces too small for realism to count.
The game plays offline, so a face cannot depend on a server at the moment it appears.
The generative path gives the most photoreal faces, while it also brings store disclosure and the backlash against AI art.
A library of finished images is the cheapest route to realism, but a finished image cannot age.
Keeping one identity across ages with AI tools needs face-recognition weights that the licence rule forbids without payment.
Generating on the player's PC removes the server, but about half of players lack the graphics card for it.
Generative AI stays in scope; both generation on the player PC and studio-only generation are evaluated, and a route with no generative AI is not the lead.
items.why: The person wants to weigh the two AI placements before choosing.
items.accepted-risk: Either placement means a Steam AI disclosure and exposure to the backlash against AI art; generation on the PC also needs written guardrails.

items.text: All four Football Manager complaints matter: the plastic look, no aging, clones, and faces wrong for the nation.
items.why: The person picked every complaint.

items.text: The first version makes faces read as real people and makes every regen look individual; aging and the fit to a nation must be acceptable, not excellent.
items.why: The person picked the plastic look and the clones as the two complaints to solve best.

items.text: Faces are photoreal by default, with a painted portrait style as a player setting.
items.why: The person chose both looks.
items.accepted-risk: Two looks to build and keep consistent for every face at every age.

items.text: The player profile, at about 200 to 300 pixels, sets the detail bar for every face.
items.why: The person chose the profile as the key screen.

items.text: A first version whose identity lives only in a finished image makes aging later need a new identity basis, while the first targets favour finished images.
From the first version, every face stores an identity that can age, even if the first version ages it only lightly; photo quality and variety still come first.
items.why: The person chose aging-ready over a photo-only identity, so faces in existing saves never change when aging arrives.

items.text: Which identity basis holds one person across ages: a genome with an AI pass, licensed AI identity tools, a seed with an age slider, or a model we train?
Does an AI pass also run on the player PC, now that studio AI already makes the textures?
The lead identity basis is a face genome on a 3D head, aged by rules, with a light AI pass that paints photoreal skin, hair, and light; the other three bases are not taken further now.
items.why: The person chose it alone from the four explained options.
items.accepted-risk: The most engineering of the four; hair and the licence of the tools that make the AI follow the render are unproven.

items.text: AI works only in the studio: it makes libraries of skin, eye, and hair textures by age, and the game renderer puts them on genome heads, so no AI runs on the player PC.
A PC without a capable graphics card shows the genome render in the painted style, so every PC has a face and only the photo finish needs the graphics card.
Which tools that make an image model follow a render (depth or edge guides) allow commercial use with FLUX.1 schnell or SDXL?
Where the photo finish runs stays open until the renderer and hair are better understood.
items.why: The person has no preference yet.

items.text: The head model is FLAME 2023 Open for identity shape, with MakeHuman CC0 age and body targets adapted onto it, all running in our own code so regens are created during play.
items.why: The person wants the most control on a commercial-safe base.
items.accepted-risk: Fitting the MakeHuman targets onto the FLAME mesh is our own work, and FLAME skin textures need a separate licence check.

items.text: Age lives in the 3D head, both shape and surface: bone growth, fat shift, wrinkles, pores, grey hair, and hairline; the AI pass only paints and must not change the age.
items.why: The person wants aging predictable and owned.
items.accepted-risk: Wrinkle and skin sets for each decade across every skin tone are a large art job, and the AI pass must be tuned so it never repaints the age.

items.text: MakeHuman bundled assets, including morph targets, are CC0, and exports carry no limitation.
Which licence covers FLAME skin textures, and do we need our own skin textures?
AI in the studio can make the wrinkle and skin sets for each decade and skin tone, which shrinks the art job that aging in 3D creates.
Regens are born during play, so the head model must create heads in our code at run time; a tool that makes heads only in its own editor, such as MetaHuman, cannot serve that.
items.evidence: MetaHuman creates characters in MetaHuman Creator; https://www.metahuman.com/license

items.text: The summary at the first check-in is right as written.
items.why: The person confirmed it and chose hair and beards next.

items.text: Hair type, colour, density, and hairline are genes in the genome; hairstyle is a choice that can change while the person stays recognisable.
A regen changes hairstyle at set life moments, such as a first-team debut, a transfer, or retirement, and keeps it between them.
items.why: Fewer changes, and each one tells a story.

items.text: Hair is built as hair cards in 3D, authored per style.
items.why: The person wants hair fully in 3D and predictable.
items.accepted-risk: Each style is art work, and hair cards are known to render tightly coiled hair badly, which feeds the faces-wrong-for-the-nation complaint.

items.text: Beards use the same hair-card method as the hair.
items.why: One system to build.

items.text: Hair cards suit straight and wavy hair, while a large share of footballers have tightly coiled hair that cards render badly.
Is stubble a hair card or a skin texture inside the one beard system?
Coiled hair gets dedicated authoring: braids and locs as geometry, fades and cornrows as scalp textures.
items.why: Coiled hair must look right, or the game repeats the wrong-for-the-nation complaint.

items.text: Hairstyle can change at a first-team debut, a transfer, turning about 30, retirement, and club milestones (trophies, captaincy, appearance landmarks, big occasions), and each regen has his own tendency, so some change often and some never.
items.why: The person picked every moment and said the moments are not uniform for all players.

items.text: Code generates the structure of hair and skin; AI in the studio makes the textures; no artists are involved; the person reviews every result.
items.why: The person wants the art pipeline in code and studio AI, with a single human reviewer.
items.accepted-risk: The person is the only quality gate for 150 or more styles and every skin set, and studio AI trained on skewed data is weakest on coiled hair and dark skin, where the representation risk is highest; the textures also add to the Steam disclosure.

items.text: The first version ships 150 or more hairstyles across all hair types.
items.why: Rare repeats across a whole save.
items.accepted-risk: The largest art job, with the most coiled-hair authoring.

items.text: A hidden style trait per regen sets how often he changes his look, and it can link to personality: a showman changes often, a quiet professional never.
The art pipeline prints review sheets: a grid of every style across every hair type, skin tone, and age, so gaps and bias show at a glance for the one reviewer.
Regens come from real countries, so a face must fit real populations, including diaspora and mixed heritage.
items.why: The person chose real countries over fictional nations.
items.accepted-risk: Mapping real nations to looks carries the ethics and stereotype risks of real demographics.

items.text: Does the whole game use real countries (leagues, international football, eligibility), and does the season design record it?
All four origin failures are equally unacceptable: a look wrong for the nation, one look per nation, missing diaspora and mixed heritage, and coarse skin tone.
items.why: The person chose all four.

items.text: Each regen carries a mix of ancestry proportions, and each gene draws from the pools in the mix.
items.why: Mixed heritage and variety come naturally.
items.accepted-risk: Gene pool data is needed for every ancestry region.

items.text: The regens of a nation follow the ancestry spread of its real professional footballers, not its general population.
items.why: The most football-true result.

items.text: Spreads come from published data where it exists, and the judgement of the person fills the gaps and is recorded as judgement.
items.why: Data first, judgement only where data is missing.

items.text: Heritage shapes the face and also gives a regen a second nation for international football.
items.why: A real football mechanic that links faces to the season layer.

items.text: Where does heritage-based international eligibility live in the season and international design?
Spreads should follow footballers, while published ancestry data describes populations, and inferring the ancestry of real players from photos is not acceptable.
Population data sets the base spread, and public birthplace and eligibility records of professional players shift each nation towards its diaspora; no faces of real players are used.
items.why: Heritage evidence without looking at anyone.

items.text: Family looks (sons, nephews, and brothers of retired players) come after the first version; the genome stores what they need from the start.
items.why: The person wants them, but not in the first version.

items.text: The product rule says illustration is generated in code and not sourced from image files, while studio AI textures for skin and hair would ship as image files.
Skin and hair textures ship as compact data, parameters and small detail tiles, that code expands into full textures, which keeps the spirit of the rule against shipped illustration files.
items.why: A middle path between amending the rule and generating everything at run time.

items.text: FLUX.1 schnell has about 12 billion parameters, so even a compressed copy is a download of several gigabytes; SDXL-class models are about 7 GB.
Where the photo finish is not available, the player chooses in settings between the painted style and our best render with studio textures.
items.why: The person chose the player choice.

items.text: Segmind Vega (about 0.74 billion parameters) and T2I-Adapter depth guides (about 77 million) are both Apache-2.0, so a render-guided photo finish can ship in about 1.5 to 2 GB.
SD 1.5 and its distilled forms such as BK-SDM Tiny are CreativeML OpenRAIL-M, which allows commercial shipping with the use-restriction notice passed on, in about 1 to 2 GB.
SD-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo, Sana-Sprint, and the pretrained img2img-turbo weights cannot ship in a sold game without a paid agreement.
Our own distilled finisher, a small one-step model trained on studio FLUX.1 schnell finishes of our renders, replaces Vega after the first version.
items.why: The person kept the order: Vega at launch, the distilled finisher later.

items.text: No public source gives speeds for a 512 pixel, one-to-four-step, render-guided pass on consumer graphics cards, so the choice needs our own benchmark.
An AI pass runs on capable player PCs: Segmind Vega with a T2I-Adapter depth guide first, replaced by our own distilled finisher when it beats Vega.
items.why: Off the shelf now, smaller and on-look later.
items.accepted-risk: Steam treats the pass as live generation, which needs a written account of guardrails, and speed on consumer PCs is unmeasured.

items.text: The finisher is an optional download, offered in settings when the graphics card can run it.
items.why: A small base game, and the photo look is opt-in.

items.text: Faces are photoreal by default, while the photo finish is an optional download, so a player without it never sees the default look.
The default look is our best render with studio textures; the finisher upgrades it to photo on capable PCs that download it; the painted style stays a setting.
items.why: An optional finisher cannot be the default.

items.text: Likeness to real footballers is checked by studio audits of thousands of sample faces before release; nothing screens at run time.
items.why: Avoids the face-recognition licence at run time.
items.accepted-risk: A face that resembles a real footballer can still appear in a save, since nothing screens at run time.

items.text: The finisher decision says Vega first and our distilled finisher later, while the area close puts the distilled finisher in the first version.
At 3,000 to 10,000 regens a season over 30 seasons, baking six ages of every face at about 40 KB is roughly 20 to 70 GB, so a save cannot store every face in advance.
items.evidence: estimate from the regen counts in the research pass

items.text: Faces render in a separate Rust portrait process (wgpu off-screen, with the finisher beside it through ONNX Runtime), which hands images to the page and keeps graphics out of the simulation.
items.why: Keeps the simulation process clean.
items.accepted-risk: A third process to ship, start, and supervise beside the engine and the window.

items.text: The current-age face of each followed player (squad and shortlist) is baked and stored; every other face is drawn on demand and cached.
items.why: A small save, with no delay on the faces the manager sees most.

items.text: How does the portrait process fit the app package (a Tauri sidecar) and the packaging plan of one interface with two paths?
A followed player gets a new baked face at age-band edges and at life moments, not every season or birthday.
items.why: The fewest renders.
items.accepted-risk: Aging shows as visible steps between bands.

items.text: The painted style is a painterly shader on the render in the portrait process, with no AI, so it runs on every PC and gives players who avoid AI art a clean choice.
items.why: No AI at all, on every PC.

items.text: Where do the age-band edges fall?
Every face outside the followed players is drawn on demand, while the finisher may be slow, so a list of unfollowed players could stall if each face waits for the finisher.
Lists show the render at once, and the finisher upgrades faces in the background as each one finishes.
items.why: A slow finisher must never stall a list.

items.text: Aging runs from 15 to 70, through coaching and management.
items.why: The game shows former players as staff for decades.
items.accepted-risk: The most age sets for the head, including the changes of the 60s.

items.text: Band edges follow career stages: academy, breakthrough, peak, veteran, retired, and staff decades.
items.why: The bands tell the career story.
items.accepted-risk: Long gaps at peak, and the academy stage covers the years when a face changes most.

items.text: Two life events mark the face: weight gain or loss after football, and faster greying for a manager under pressure; injury marks and tattoos are not included.
items.why: The person picked these two.

items.text: Career-stage bands put the academy in one stage, while a face changes most from 15 to 21.
Which game data drives weight after football and stress greying (personality, lifestyle, job pressure), and where is it designed?
The academy has two stages, 15 to 17 and 18 to 20, before the career stages.
items.why: A face changes most while bone growth ends.

items.text: If the art job forces a cut, hair loss moves to later first; teenage growth, fat shift, wrinkles and skin, and greying stay.
items.why: The person chose hair loss as the first to go.

items.text: Every closed area keeps every decision in the first version, while one person reviews all art and no budget limits the first version.
No limit is set on the first version: every kept decision ships in it.
items.why: The person chose no limit.
items.accepted-risk: The first version is large for one reviewer and may take long to ship, with no budget to force the order.

items.text: The painted style is offered as a clean choice for players who avoid AI art, while it paints textures that studio AI made.
The painted mode is a look, not an AI choice, and the game makes no AI claim about it.
items.why: A false no-AI claim is the worst outcome in a backlash.

items.text: The game is open by design about faces: the Steam disclosure, a plain explanation in settings that identity and age are never AI and only the paint is, and a public page on how faces are made, including the likeness audits and the data rules.
items.why: Openness is the best defence against the backlash.

items.text: The settings text says identity and age are never AI, while the wrinkle and skin textures that show age are made by studio AI.
The openness text says precisely that code decides who a player is and how old he looks, studio AI made the skin and hair materials, and the optional finisher paints light and skin.
items.why: A partly false never-AI claim would feed the backlash.
